identity.title: Improving the Scaling Laws of Synthetic Data with Deliberate Practice

problem.claim: Improve the sample efficiency and scaling of synthetic-data generation.

gap.claim: Naively scaling synthetic data produces diminishing returns, while generating large datasets and pruning afterward is inefficient.

contributions.claim: Proposes Deliberate Practice for Synthetic Data Generation (DP), which dynamically targets informative synthetic samples.
Provides a theoretical account of how training on challenging, informative examples can improve scaling laws.
Reports improved scaling performance using substantially fewer samples and training iterations than prior work.

stated_novelty.claim: DP is presented as a novel framework that directly approximates the generation of informative samples instead of pruning a large generated dataset afterward.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that on ImageNet-100, DP uses 3.4× fewer samples and six times fewer iterations while achieving superior performance compared with prior work.
The authors report that on ImageNet-1k, DP uses 8× fewer samples and reduces iterations by 30%, while achieving superior performance compared with prior work.
The authors report theoretical and empirical support for improved scaling from challenging, informative examples.

narrative_sequence.summary: Synthetic-data scaling is described as difficult because simply adding data yields diminishing returns.
Pruning is identified as a way to emphasize informative samples, but DP instead approximates their direct generation.
DP applies deliberate-practice-inspired dynamic synthetic-data generation to improve sample efficiency.
The abstract reports theoretical analysis and ImageNet-100/ImageNet-1k results showing lower data and iteration requirements with superior performance versus prior work.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects its method to a human-learning principle, then operationalizes that principle as dynamically generated challenging and informative examples rather than post-hoc pruning.

lessons.interpretation: A motivating analogy is most useful when translated into a concrete data-selection or generation mechanism.
lessons.application: When proposing a learning strategy inspired by another domain, explicitly map the principle to the mechanism that produces the claimed training signal.
lessons.exception: This move is unsuitable when the analogy cannot yield an operational mechanism or when the target domain lacks a measurable notion of informative difficulty.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the theoretical assumptions, scaling-law form, evaluation metrics, prior-work baselines, or statistical details behind the reported comparisons.
It does not explain how DP identifies challenging or informative samples or whether the reported savings generalize beyond the two ImageNet settings.
